primary_topics: Keynote address and induction of the Association of Certified Public Accountants in Public Practice (ACPAPP), January 29, 2008 -- accepted only because ACPAPP's president Reynaldo Altre reminded CJP that Altre's firm has been auditing CJP's group of companies for 40 years since 1968

The three mandates of CPAs and civil society in the liberty-and-prosperity framework: (1) the courts as great equalizers for civil liberties (strict scrutiny); (2) the irony that lawyers know more about protecting civil liberties than about nurturing prosperity -- despite the Constitution's mandate to alleviate the poor; (3) ACPAPP as part of civil society that assists the three branches of government in uplifting people from misgovernance

CJP's judicial vision: four Ins (integrity, independence, industry, intelligence); plague of ships (kinship, relationship, friendship, fellowship); ACID problems (access, corruption, incompetence, delay); twin goals of liberty and prosperity
Call to ACPAPP: join the search for 'jobs and justice, food and freedom, investments and integrity, economics and ethics, development and democracy; in short, Liberty and Prosperity'
sub_topics: Accepted because of 40-year relationship: 'your president reminded me that he and his firm have been the auditors of our small group of companies for about 40 years already, since 1968. So, I could not refuse.'

Vision as CJ: four Ins (integrity, independence, industry, intelligence); morally courageous against influence, interference and indifference; plague of ships (kinship, relationship, friendship, fellowship); ACID problems (access, corruption, incompetence, delay); twin goals of liberty and prosperity under the rule of law

Courts as great equalizers: 'it is easy to see the role of courts as the great equalizers between the citizens and the government. The battle for civil liberties is a never-ending saga of trials and triumphs for the judiciary and for our people.'

The irony on prosperity: 'how much lawyers know about protecting civil liberties seems to be negatively correlated with how little they have thus far devoted to nurturing the prosperity of our people. This is the reality that persists despite the Mandates of the 1987 Constitution: to alleviate the plight of the marginalized and the poor; to promote a just and dynamic social order that will ensure the prosperity and independence of the nation and free the people from poverty; and to achieve a more equitable distribution of opportunities, income and wealth.'

Prosperity requires as much nurturing: 'I am truly convinced that the prosperity of our people requires as much nurturing in the present century as that accorded to liberty in the past. To be relevant, courts must be constantly attuned to the needs of the present and the vagaries of the future.'

ACPAPP as civil society: 'civil society has been in the forefront of the fight for liberty. Popular action has brought down a dictatorship; it has also rejected a once populist, but later perceived to be corrupt, administration.'

Call to ACPAPP: 'ACPAPP as a microcosm of civil society has a big stake in ensuring the liberty and prosperity of our people... Please join me in tirelessly searching and fearlessly espousing both jobs and justice, food and freedom, investments and integrity, economics and ethics, development and democracy; in short, Liberty and Prosperity.'

The Constitution mandates both liberty AND prosperity; the legal profession has excelled at the first while largely ignoring the second.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered January 29, 2008 as inducting officer and keynote at the ACPAPP (Association of Certified Public Accountants in Public Practice) -- accepted only because President Reynaldo Altre reminded CJP that Altre's firm has been auditing CJP's companies for 40 years since 1968 ('So, I could not refuse') -- this address applies the liberty-and-prosperity philosophy to the CPA profession and civil society. CJP restates his judicial vision (four Ins: integrity, independence, industry, intelligence; plague of ships: kinship, relationship, friendship, fellowship; ACID problems: access, corruption, incompetence, delay; twin goals of liberty and prosperity under the rule of law). He notes the courts' role as 'great equalizers' for civil liberties, then identifies the legal profession's blind spot: 'how much lawyers know about protecting civil liberties seems to be negatively correlated with how little they have thus far devoted to nurturing the prosperity of our people' -- despite the Constitution's explicit mandates to alleviate the poor, promote a just and dynamic social order, and achieve equitable distribution of opportunities, income and wealth. 'I am truly convinced that the prosperity of our people requires as much nurturing in the present century as that accorded to liberty in the past.' ACPAPP as civil society: 'civil society has been in the forefront of the fight for liberty. Popular action has brought down a dictatorship; it has also rejected a once populist, but later perceived to be corrupt, administration.' Closing call: 'Please join me in tirelessly searching and fearlessly espousing both jobs and justice, food and freedom, investments and integrity, economics and ethics, development and democracy; in short, Liberty and Prosperity.'
